summary: Covers fundamentals to understand when defining, interpreting or implementing ways to control user expectations over the Internet. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A talk about how to make sure users know what to expect from the network.

subtitle: A framework for understanding the fundamentals of user agreements and acceptable use policies on the Internet.

tldr.problem: As the Internet expands to serve schools, businesses, and diverse communities, networks need clear policies to define user expectations, but best practices for designing these policies are often unclear.
tldr.mechanism: This memo identifies three core relationship zones (where you get service from, who your peers are, who you serve to) and lists issues that should be considered when formulating acceptable use policies, then shows a detailed example from the CoVis educational networking project.
tldr.outcome: The framework helps network operators clarify their rules, users understand what to expect, and both avoid misunderstandings and potential legal conflict.

facts.label: CoVis services
facts.value: Email, Telnet, FTP, Gopher, Usenet news, video conferencing, screen sharing

today: RFC 1746 is informational. The framework it describes remains relevant today. Schools and networks continue to use similar principles for user agreements, though the emphasis on student privacy and parental authority anticipated modern child safety debates by decades. The CoVis policy was groundbreaking for its era and established patterns that influenced later K-12 acceptable use policies.

sections.title: Understanding Acceptable Use Policies
sections.content:
An acceptable use policy (AUP) is a set of rules a network operator gives to its users, defining expected and prohibited behavior. Every network has one, whether written or implicit. AUPs have become increasingly important as the Internet grows and serves new communities: K-12 schools, corporate networks, research institutions, and community organizations all need to set expectations about what the network is for and what users can do.

The memo covers fundamental concepts needed to formulate a coherent AUP. The authors, Bill Manning and Don Perkins, argue that a well-designed policy protects both users and providers, clarifies the purpose of the network, and helps the community understand its role within the larger Internet.
sections.eli5: Every network needs rules. This note is about how to think through what those rules should be and why they matter.

sections.title: Three Relationship Zones
sections.content:
A sound AUP addresses three critical relationships that shape what a network can offer and what policies make sense.

Where you get service from. Most networks receive service from upstream providers—either transit (connectivity to the wider Internet) or raw circuits. These providers have their own agreements specifying terms and conditions. Your AUP must be consistent with your upstream providers' policies, because you cannot offer more freedom to your users than you are permitted to have.

Who your peers are. Peers are networks at your level that you interconnect with or compete with. Your policies should be consistent with peers to foster collaborative communities. But it is also important to explicitly identify the community you serve and the values that define it.

Who you provide service to. Finally, you must clearly inform your own users (end users, departments, schools, or organizations) what policies apply to them. Without clear communication, users will misunderstand what is allowed, and disputes are likely. The memo stresses that policies should reflect the actual community standards of the network's users.
sections.eli5: Think about three questions: (1) who gives you Internet access and what rules did they give you? (2) what rules do your neighbors use? (3) what do your users need to know?

sections.title: Key Issues to Address
sections.content:
Beyond the three core relationships, the memo lists considerations that should be analyzed and balanced in any AUP design.

These include: privacy (what communications are private and what may be monitored), freedom of expression, safety (protection from harassment), legal constraints (compliance with applicable laws), security requirements (protecting the system from misuse), ethical standards, plagiarism and copyright, resource utilization (preventing abuse that overburdens systems), indemnification (liability questions), and remedies for violations.

The authors stress that policies must balance conflicting demands: providing access and security, fostering open communication while protecting the network's capability. Designing policy involves analyzing these tensions and arriving at a synthesis appropriate for your community. The memo emphasizes that one size does not fit all—a K-12 school network has different needs and values than a research institution or corporate network.
sections.eli5: Good policies think about hard questions: what counts as private, what happens if someone breaks the rules, how do you stop spam, what's fair use, and who pays if something goes wrong.

sections.title: Case Study: The CoVis Project
sections.content:
To illustrate how these principles apply, the RFC includes an extensive example from the CoVis (Collaborative Visualization) Project, an NSF-funded educational network connecting high school students and scientists for collaborative research.

CoVis granted all students full Internet accounts with access to all standard Internet services—email, Usenet news, Telnet, FTP, gopher—plus specialized tools for real-time collaboration and video conferencing. This openness created safety, privacy, and behavioral challenges absent in traditional classroom networks.

The CoVis policy addressed these by drawing on analogies: the American Library Association's Library Bill of Rights (for access principles), school conduct codes (for standards of behavior), and professional ethics codes (for privacy and freedom of expression). The policy gave students privacy in email and collaborative tools unless suspected of policy violation. It prohibited offensive language and personal attacks, set standards for copyright compliance and network use for illegal activities, and made clear that school conduct codes applied online. Crucially, the policy clarified that parents, not the school, have final authority over their child's access restrictions—mirroring library practice.
sections.eli5: The CoVis example shows how one school network balanced giving students real Internet access while setting clear rules about respect, privacy, and safety—learning from libraries and school codes.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The memo concludes that as the Internet becomes more diverse and interconnected, clear user expectations are essential. Networks that fail to communicate their policies risk user confusion, disputes, and legal liability. The three relationship zones provide a framework for thinking through the constraints and opportunities of your network.

The authors note that internetworking—connecting schools, students, and diverse communities to a global network—is fundamentally different from closed or proprietary systems. It requires policies that balance openness with responsibility, access with protection. The memo invites feedback and frames its example policies as contributions to an evolving field.
sections.eli5: As more communities use the Internet, clear rules are more important, not less. Good policies explain your values and earn users' trust.
